headline: High: Pipecat’s allowlisted network egress can exfiltrate Great Expectations outputs if wired together, while shared-bus concurrency raises conflict and cascading-error risk.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Great Expectations exposes files for data sources, validation results, and documentation, while Pipecat can ingest text and conversation state over stdin/stdout and shared bus. A prompt-injection path exists only if Great Expectations outputs are manually or programmatically fed into Pipecat as instructions; no default shared channel is documented, so this stays low.
conditions: IF Great Expectations output is copied into Pipecat prompts or messages
IF a shared bus carries validation text from agent_a into agent_b without provenance filtering
mitigations: Separate the agents onto distinct channels with no automatic text handoff
Prefix all Great Expectations output as untrusted data in Pipecat prompts
Add a simple allowlist that strips imperative phrases before forwarding
Use a human review step before any agent_b action on agent_a text

B_data_leakage.rationale: Great Expectations touches validation results and documentation, and Pipecat has allowlisted network egress plus many third-party API integrations. If agent_a outputs are routed into agent_b’s context, agent_b can transmit them off-box by default through its service connectors. The pairwise leakage pathway is plausible in default Pipecat deployments, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF Great Expectations validation results are passed into Pipecat context or memory
IF Pipecat is configured with any external STT/LLM/TTS provider
mitigations: Disable external providers in Pipecat for the shared workflow
Redact validation outputs before they reach agent_b
Keep Great Expectations artifacts in a separate workspace
Turn off logging for any fields that may contain sensitive validation data
requires-engineering: add DLP filtering on the handoff boundary

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Great Expectations can write files for validation results and documentation, and Pipecat supports shared-bus session state with multiple instances. Overlapping writes to shared artifacts or state can race unless the orchestrator adds locking. Because both agents can mutate shared workflow state, conflict risk exists in default multi-instance use.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same workspace or artifact path
IF multiple Pipecat instances share the same bus without external locking
mitigations: Assign separate output directories per agent
Serialize writes through a single coordinator
Enable file locking on shared artifacts
Avoid shared mutable state for validation outputs
requires-engineering: add optimistic-concurrency checks

D_cascading_error.rationale: Great Expectations produces validation results that Pipecat can consume as text or conversation state. If Pipecat treats those outputs as authoritative, a bad validation or malformed documentation can cascade into downstream actions or responses. The interaction is plausible but not directly documented, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF Pipecat uses Great Expectations output as an input prompt or decision signal
IF no verification step checks the validation result before downstream use
mitigations: Insert a verification step before Pipecat consumes validation output
Require structured schemas for any handoff between agents
Mark Great Expectations output as advisory only
Log and compare source data against the rendered summary
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks

E_compliance.rationale: Great Expectations touches validation results and documentation, while Pipecat touches audio, video, images, text, and analytics/metrics and can send data to external providers. No residency or certification mismatch is documented in either profile, so only a low compliance gap is supportable from the profiles alone; the other agent is cited because the risk arises from the pair’s data flow.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed from Great Expectations into Pipecat providers
IF retention or residency requirements apply to the shared workflow
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Pipecat-connected flows
Review provider residency settings before enabling them
Minimize retained analytics and conversation logs
Document the data classes allowed across the boundary
requires-engineering: enforce residency-aware routing
